name: Progressivism
actions: An early-1900s reform movement responding to industrialization's problems through government regulation, social activism, and political reform.

name: Ida B. Wells
actions: Tennessean for a time and journalist
She was an anti-lynching crusader, and suffragist.
Founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago, one of the first organizations for Black women voters and co-founded the NAACP
She challenged racism within the suffrage movement while fighting for universal rights.

name: Boss Tweed
actions: Corrupt leader of New York's Tammany Hall political machine, a symbol of political boss corruption.

name: Andrew Carnegie
actions: Carnegie built a steel empire in the late 1800s: Carnegie Steel. He used the Bessemer Process to make steel more efficiently and stronger. A believer in charity, he gave much of his fortune away, especially to educational foundations.

name: Assembly Line
actions: A manufacturing process popularized by Henry Ford that dramatically sped up production and lowered the cost of goods.

name: Muckraker
actions: A journalist who investigated and exposed corruption, corporate abuses, and social problems in the early 1900s.

name: Factory
actions: A centralized site of industrial production, often associated with long hours, low wages, and dangerous working conditions.

name: Labor Union
actions: An organization of workers formed to negotiate collectively with employers over wages, hours, and working conditions.

name: Political Boss
actions: A powerful, often corrupt figure who controlled a political machine and traded favors or patronage for votes.

name: Corruption
actions: The abuse of political or economic power for private gain, a central target of Progressive Era reformers.

name: Reform
actions: Organized efforts to improve social, political, or economic conditions, a defining feature of the Progressive Era.

name: Tenement
actions: Crowded, often unsafe multi-family housing common in industrial-era cities, and a target of housing reform.

name: Political Primary
actions: An election in which party members vote to select their candidate for office.

name: John D. Rockefeller
actions: In 1863, Rockefeller entered the oil refining business and created the Standard Oil Company. He bought up most of the other oil refining companies in the US so that by 1879, his company Standard Oil controlled 90% of the nation’s oil business. Later, his company was broken up into smaller companies by the US government, including ExxonMobil, Chevron and Conoco.

name: Urbanization
actions: Urbanization is the process where more people move from rural or country areas to live and work in cities and towns.

name: Cornelius Vanderbilt
actions: Vanderbilt got his start in the steamboat business, but in 1862 he began buying railroad lines, which became the source of most of his wealth.

name: JP Morgan
actions: JP Morgan was one of the wealthiest financiers and bankers in the US. He was largely responsible for the formation of large corporations like General Electric and US Steel. He even helped save the US from financial ruin by loaning the US government money on two separate occasions.

name: Thomas Edison
actions: Thomas Edison invented and patented the modern electric light bulb in the 1870s.

name: Industry
actions: The type of specialty a specific business specializes in.

name: Monopoly
actions: This is when a company controls all aspects of an industry, allowing them to set prices unfairly and take advantage of consumers

name: Wealth Gap
actions: Wealth inequality is the unequal distribution of assets among individuals, groups, or organisations within a society or country.

name: Settlement Houses
actions: community centers in poor urban areas where middle-class volunteer workers lived to help low-income families and immigrants

name: Pure Food and Drug Act
actions: The Pure Food and Drug Act was passed in 1906 stating that it was “for preventing the manufacture, sale, or transportation of adulterated or misbranded or poisonous or deleterious foods, drugs, medicines, and liquors, and for regulating traffic therein, and for other purposes.”

name: Social Darwinism
actions: The application of "survival of the fittest" to justify economic inequality.

name: Secret Ballot
actions: Voters were less subject to pressure and intimidation when they could vote in secret

name: Recall
actions: Elected officials could be removed from office by voters in a special election

name: Direct Primary
actions: Special elections were held to determine whom party members wanted to represent them as candidates in the general election

name: Direct Election of Senators
actions: Senators were elected directly by the people (17th Amendment) instead of being chosen by state legislatures

name: Referendum
actions: Voters could compel legislators to place a bill on the ballot for approval

name: Conservation
actions: Conservation is the responsible care, protection, and sustainable use of Earth's natural resources to prevent depletion, waste, and harm

name: Trustbusting
actions: Trustbusting was the act of the government breaking up large companies that controlled too much of an industry. This stopped one company from getting too powerful which hurts consumers.

name: Meat Inspection Act
actions: makes it illegal to sell adulterated or misbranded meat and ensures that livestock are slaughtered and processed under sanitary conditions

name: Collective Bargaining
actions: This is the main tool unions use. It means workers negotiate as one united group with management, rather than each person speaking alone. The final deal is written into a legal contract.

name: Upton Sinclair
actions: Muckraking journalist whose novel The Jungle (1906) exposed unsanitary conditions in the meatpacking industry, leading to federal food safety laws.

name: Elections
actions: People voting to elect mayors, representatives, and other polititions

name: Ida Tarbell
actions: Muckraking journalist whose investigative reporting on Standard Oil helped spur antitrust action against Rockefeller's monopoly.

name: Lincoln Steffens
actions: Muckraking journalist known for The Shame of the Cities, exposing political corruption in urban government.

name: Jacob Riis
actions: Photojournalist and reformer whose How the Other Half Lives documented slum conditions in New York City tenements.

name: National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA)
actions: Focused on a state-by-state approach to win voting rights for women in local elections before pursuing federal change.
traditional and moderate methods
lobbying politicians
circulating petitions

name: National Woman’s Party (NWP)
actions: Demanded an immediate federal constitutional amendment to enfranchise all American women at once
Used militant and confrontational tactics
Public parades
Mass protests
Picketing the White House
Enduring voluntary imprisonment and hunger strikes.

name: Alice Paul
actions: NWP

organized parades, pickets, and hunger strikes. She was arrested for her activism and endured harsh isolation, force feeding, and other forms of torture in prison. Her bold tactics kept suffrage in the headlines and pressured lawmakers to act.

name: Carrie Chapman Catt
actions: NAWSA

succeeded Susan B. Anthony as president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA). Ever the optimist, she later found the League of Women Voters. shortly before the final ratification was complete.

name: Susan B. Anthony
actions: NAWSA

One of the most recognizable figures of the suffrage movement, Anthony co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association and later presided over the National American Woman Suffrage Association as well. She traveled the country for decades organizing, giving speeches, lobbying lawmakers, and laying the groundwork for future generations to succeed.

name: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
actions: NAWSA

central to the first women’s rights convention in Seneca Falls in 1848 and authored it’s Declaration of Sentiments. A powerful writer and thinker, she provided much of the philosophical foundation for women’s equality.

name: Seneca Falls Convention
actions: The Seneca Falls Convention was the first formal women's rights convention in United States history, held on July 19–20, 1848, at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York. [1] (https://www.history.com/articles/seneca-falls-convention), [2] (https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/seneca-falls-convention-setting-national-stage-womens-suffrage)

name: Civil Disobedience
actions: Breaking the law to show its injustice
Public to gain awareness
Nonviolent

name: María Adelina Isabel Emilia Otero-Warren
actions: NWP
She weader in New Mexico’s woman’s suffrage movement.
She spearheaded the lobbying effort to ratify the 19th Amendment in New Mexico.

name: American Dream
actions: The American Dream is the national belief that anyone, regardless of where they were born or their social class, can achieve success, prosperity, and upward mobility through hard work and determination.

name: Segregation
actions: Racial segregation is the separation of people into racial or other ethnic groups in daily life.
Segregation can involve the spatial separation of the races, and mandatory use of different institutions, such as schools and hospitals by people of different races.

name: Lynching
actions: A lynching is the public killing of an individual who has not received any due process. These executions were often carried out by lawless mobs, though police officers did participate, under the pretext of justice.

name: Discrimination
actions: the unfair or unequal treatment of a person or group based on specific personal characteristics. [1] (https://www.apa.org/topics/racism-bias-discrimination/types-stress), [2] (https://study.com/academy/lesson/video/what-is-discrimination-definition-examples-quiz.html)

name: Marginalized
actions: Marginalized means treated as unimportant, powerless, or pushed to the outer edges of a society or group

name: Jim Crow
actions: Jim Crow was the name of the racial caste system which operated primarily, but not exclusively in southern and border states, between 1877 and the mid-1960s.

name: Literacy Test
actions: A literacy test is an examination that assesses a person's ability to read, write, and understand written material. This was used to restrict people's write to vote and enter the country as immigrants

name: Immigrant
actions: A person who moves who moves their residence from one country to another

name: Nativism
actions: Nativism is a political belief that favors native-born people over immigrants

name: Xenophobic
actions: showing an extreme dislike or fear of people from foreign countries

name: Activist
actions: a person who takes vigorous action to support or oppose political, social, economic, or environmental change.

name: Suffrage
actions: The right to vote

name: Imperialism
actions: A policy in which a country extends its power by taking control of other countries or territories.

name: Queen Liliuokalani
actions: The last monarch of Hawaii, who was overthrown by American businessmen in 1893.

name: Sanford B. Dole
actions: An American businessman and politician who helped overthrow Hawaii's queen and later became president of the Republic of Hawaii.

name: coup
actions: A sudden and often illegal takeover of a government by a small group.

name: American Territory
actions: Land controlled by the United States that is not a state.

name: Annex
actions: To add a territory or country to another country.

name: self-governance
actions: The ability of a people or territory to govern itself.

name: M.A.N.I.A.
actions: Militarism, Alliances, Nationalism, Imperialism, and Assassination—the main causes of World War I.

name: Nationalism
actions: Strong pride in and loyalty to one's country or nation.

name: Alliance
actions: An agreement between countries to help and support each other.

name: Propaganda
actions: Information, often biased or misleading, used to influence people's opinions or actions.

name: Sinking of the Lusitania
actions: The 1915 sinking of the British passenger ship Lusitania by a German submarine, killing nearly 1,200 people, including 128 Americans.

name: Zimmerman Telegram
actions: A secret 1917 message from Germany asking Mexico to join Germany against the United States in exchange for help getting back land lost to the U.S.

name: Trench Warfare
actions: A type of fighting in which soldiers fought from deep ditches called trenches for protection from enemy fire.

name: Chemical Warfare
actions: The use of poisonous gases or other chemicals as weapons during war.

name: Charles Schenck
actions: A man who was arrested during World War I for encouraging people to resist the military draft; his case led to the Supreme Court's decision in Schenck v. United States.

name: Elizabeth Baer
actions: An American woman who was arrested during World War I for speaking and writing against the war and the government; her case raised questions about freedom of speech during wartime.

name: Freedom of Speech
actions: The right to express ideas and opinions without unreasonable government punishment.

name: Isolationism
actions: When a nation stays isolated from others and stays out of foreign conflicts

name: feasible
actions: practical

name: menace
actions: danger, threat

name: autocratic
actions: a government where the ruler has absolute power

name: quarrel
actions: clash, feud

name: impulse
actions: urge or inspire

name: dynasties
actions: empire, regime

name: steadfast
actions: loyal, faithful

name: dominion
actions: government

name: indemnities
actions: security, guarantee

name: Name-calling
actions: Using derogatory language or insults to discredit an opponent or a competing product.
It often relies on stereotypes to create an immediate negative association.

name: Glittering generalities
actions: These are vague, high-value words that sound positive but lack a concrete definition.
Words like "freedom," "justice," or "refreshing" are used to evoke a feeling without providing evidence.

name: Transfer
actions: This technique carries the prestige and authority of a respected symbol over to a person or product.
An example is a politician standing in front of a national flag to inherit its perceived patriotism.

name: Testimonial
actions: This uses the endorsement of a celebrity or an expert to validate a claim. The goal is to make the audience trust the message because they respect the person delivering it.

name: Plain-folk
actions: This strategy attempts to convince the audience that a leader or a product is "just like them." It frames elite figures as average citizens to build rapport and relatability.

name: Card-stacking
actions: This involves selectively presenting only the positive aspects of an idea while deliberately omitting the negatives. It provides a biased and incomplete picture to the viewer.

name: Bandwagon
actions: This plays on the fear of missing out by suggesting that "everyone else is doing it." It pressures individuals to join a movement to avoid being the odd one out.

name: Disenfranchised
actions: being deprived of a right, privilege, or power, most commonly the right to vote.

name: Self Defense
actions: Defending yourself after an attack

name: Defending Democracy
actions: Many people supported joining the war because the believed they were defending democracy (governments where people vote for their leaders) accross the world.

name: Fighting for Equality
actions: The fight for equality in the United States is a long historical journey driven by marginalized groups demanding civil rights, freedom, and fair treatment under the law

name: Model T
actions: Henry Ford made the automobile affordable for the average American. By the 1920s, the growing “car culture” was changing the nation in deeper ways than even Ford might have imagined.

name: Gas Stations
actions: Automobiles encouraged the growth of related industries—especially the oil industry. The gas station—and gas fumes—became a permanent feature of the U.S. landscape.

name: Highway System
actions: By 1925, states had built hundreds of highways, and the federal government organized them into a numbered system. One of the first federal highways was Route 66, which ran from Illinois to California.

name: Vacation Industry
actions: Americans used their new cars and expanded leisure time to travel. Motels and motor camps sprung up all over the nation.

name: Advertising
actions: Ads stressed what cars gave their owners—speed, status, and a new sense of freedom.

name: Radio
actions: As more radios were sold, the radio became the centerpiece of millions of American living rooms. At first, headsets were required to listen to broadcasts.

name: Movies
actions: By the 1920s, Americans were going to the movies so often that attendance at other forms of public entertainment, such as theater, suffered. Decades later, the rise of television would have the same effect on movie attendance.

name: New Household Products
actions: Even for the majority of women who stayed at home to care for the house and children, life changed. New consumer products such as dishwashers and vacuum cleaners made housework easier.

name: Florence Allen
actions: First woman state judge (1920)

name: Marie Luhring
actions: First woman automotive engineer (1920)

name: Rebecca Felton
actions: First woman in U.S. Senate (1922)

name: Nellie Tayloe Ross
actions: First woman governor (1924)

name: Gertrude Ederle
actions: First woman to swim English Channel (1926)

name: Dorothy Arzner
actions: First woman to direct a talking movie (1927)

name: Phoebe Omie
actions: First woman to earn a federal pilot’s license (1927)

name: Charleston
actions: No fad symbolizes the Roaring Twenties more than the Charleston. Here, two young people demonstrate the wild, loose-limbed dance that swept the nation.

name: Consumerism
actions: Consumerism is a social, cultural, and economic phenomenon where personal happiness, social status, and economic health are tied to the continuous purchase and consumption of goods and services

name: Magazines
actions: Mass-market magazines with eye-catching covers were more popular than ever. This Life magazine cover (left) highlights the growing popularity of golf among both men and women. Amazing Stories (right) was the first “pulp” magazine devoted exclusively to science fiction.

name: Temperance Movement
actions: A reform movement, strongest in the 1800s and early 1900s, that urged people to drink less alcohol or quit entirely because it was blamed for crime, poverty, and broken families.

name: Prohibition
actions: The nationwide ban on making, selling, and transporting alcohol in the U.S. from 1920 to 1933, created by the 18th Amendment.

name: Vote Wet
actions: To vote in favor of legal alcohol; "wets" wanted Prohibition ended or relaxed.

name: Vote Dry
actions: To vote to keep alcohol banned; "drys" supported Prohibition.

name: Speakeasy
actions: A secret, illegal bar that sold alcohol during Prohibition.

name: Bootlegger
actions: A person who illegally made, smuggled, or sold alcohol during Prohibition.

name: Enforcement
actions: The work of government agents to make people obey a law; Prohibition enforcement was weak because of too few agents, bribery, and widespread public defiance.

name: Organized Crime
actions: Criminal groups that work together like a business, using bribery and violence to protect their profits; Prohibition gave them a huge new source of money.

name: Al Capone
actions: Chicago gang boss and the most famous Prohibition-era gangster, who made millions from bootlegging and was finally convicted of tax evasion in 1931.
